title: What medical safety and infection control training must hospitals and clinics in Japan provide?
description: Japan's Medical Care Act Enforcement Regulation Art 1-11: medical safety and infection control training about twice a year, records, and the 2026 changes.
shortAnswer: Under Article 1-11 of Japan's Medical Care Act Enforcement Regulation, every hospital, clinic and midwifery home must train staff in medical safety and in infection control. The Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) expects each to run about twice a year plus as needed, with dates, attendees and topics recorded. Drug, device and medical radiation safety training are separate duties, and hospitals must appoint a medical safety manager from April 1, 2026.
keyTakeaways: Article 6-12 of the Medical Care Act makes the manager of every hospital, clinic and midwifery home responsible for medical safety measures, expressly including staff training, and Article 1-11 of the Enforcement Regulation sets out what those measures are.

MHLW guidance says hospital-wide medical safety training and in-house infection control training should each be held periodically about twice a year (nen 2-kai teido), plus whenever needed, and that the date, attendees and topics must be recorded.

Separate training duties apply to drug safety, medical device safety (including training before any new device is used) and, since April 1, 2020, medical radiation safety for staff who perform radiological procedures.

From April 1, 2026, hospitals and inpatient facilities must appoint a full-time medical safety manager who can be directed to deliver the staff training; from April 1, 2029, managers involved in deciding whether a death is a reportable medical accident must complete designated training.
regulator: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) Health Policy Bureau, with prefectural governors and health center cities inspecting facilities
appliesTo: Managers (kanrisha) of hospitals, clinics and midwifery homes in Japan
All staff of those facilities, including physicians, nurses, pharmacists, technologists and support staff
Drug safety managers, medical device safety managers and medical radiation safety leads
Medical safety managers appointed under Article 1-11(1)(v) from April 1, 2026
Special functioning hospitals and core clinical research hospitals, which carry extra training duties

sections.heading: Where does the medical safety training duty come from?

blocks.text: The duty comes from the **Medical Care Act** (医療法, Act No. 205 of 1948) and its **Medical Care Act Enforcement Regulation** (医療法施行規則, Ministry of Health and Welfare Ordinance No. 50 of 1948). Article 6-12 of the Act requires the manager of a hospital, clinic or midwifery home to take the measures set by ministerial ordinance to secure medical safety, naming "the formulation of guidelines for securing medical safety, the implementation of training for employees" and other measures ([Medical Care Act, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/323AC0000000205)).

Article 1-11 of the Enforcement Regulation then lists those measures in two paragraphs. Paragraph 1 covers the general medical safety system: a safety guideline, a safety committee, staff training, incident reporting and improvement, a medical safety manager and safety records. Paragraph 2 adds four specific systems: in-house infection control, drug safety, medical device safety and medical radiation safety ([Enforcement Regulation, e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/323M40000100050)). Each of those systems contains its own training requirement.

The ordinance does not state how often training must run. Frequency, content and record expectations come from MHLW Health Policy Bureau notices, which local governments use when they inspect facilities. For international readers, these notices are administrative guidance (technical advice to prefectures) rather than binding law, but they are the standard inspectors apply.

sections.heading: What does Article 1-11 require for medical safety staff training?

blocks.text: Article 1-11(1)(iii) requires staff training on the basic matters and specific measures of medical safety management. The stated purpose is to improve staff awareness of medical safety, their recognition of working in cooperation with other staff, and the skills needed to work safely. The duty applies to every hospital, clinic and midwifery home, including clinics with no inpatient beds.

On March 31, 2026, MHLW reissued its guidance on Article 1-11 in notice 医政発0331第72号, replacing the medical safety section of the 2007 notice that had governed this area since the regulation took its current shape ([MHLW notice of March 31, 2026](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/10800000/001685651.pdf)). On training, the notice says:

items: training should take up concrete cases from the facility itself and should preferably be run across professions rather than by department;
training on safety content common to the whole facility should be held periodically about twice a year, and additionally whenever needed;
the facility must record what was delivered: the date and time held or attended, the attendees and the training topics; and
clinics without inpatient beds and midwifery homes without inpatient facilities may substitute training attended outside the facility, again about twice a year plus as needed.

blocks.text: The same notice confirms that the medical safety committee (required for hospitals, clinics with inpatient beds and midwifery homes with inpatient facilities) should meet about once a month and whenever a serious problem occurs. Committee findings and improvement measures must be communicated to staff, which in practice becomes a recurring input to the training program.

sections.heading: What infection control training is required?

blocks.text: Article 1-11(2)(i)(c) requires every facility to provide staff with training for in-house infection control, alongside an infection control guideline, an infection control committee (inpatient facilities only) and reporting of infection outbreaks. MHLW guidance on this item is still the 2007 Health Policy Bureau notice 医政発第0330010号 of March 30, 2007, whose infection control section was not replaced in 2026 ([MHLW notice of March 30, 2007](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/10800000/000903504.pdf)).

The 2007 notice says infection control training should teach the basic approach and concrete measures for infection control, raise each employee's awareness of infection, and build skills and team awareness. It should reflect the facility's actual circumstances and involve participation across professions. Training on infection control content common to the whole facility should be held periodically about twice a year and whenever needed, with the date, attendees and topics recorded. Outpatient-only clinics and midwifery homes may again substitute external training. The notice also permits infection control measures to be run together with the general medical safety measures, so a single combined session can satisfy both if it covers both topics and the record shows that.

sections.heading: What separate training covers drugs, devices and medical radiation?

blocks.text: Three further systems in Article 1-11(2) each carry a training duty owned by a named responsible person. The table summarizes them.

Per the 2007 notice: training before a device new to the facility is used, with a record; periodic training on devices needing skill in special functioning hospitals; content covers efficacy and safety, use, maintenance, response to malfunctions and legal requirements

blocks.text: Medical radiation safety under the Medical Care Act protects patients. Occupational protection of the staff who operate the equipment is a separate regime under the Industrial Safety and Health Act, covered in [Japan's ionizing radiation hazard prevention education](/regulations/japan-radiation-hazard-prevention-education).

sections.heading: What changed in April 2026, and what is coming in 2029?

blocks.text: MHLW Ordinance No. 27 of 2026, promulgated March 19, 2026, made two training-relevant changes. Comparing the versions of Article 1-11 on e-Gov, a new item (v) took effect on April 1, 2026, requiring hospitals, clinics with inpatient beds and midwifery homes with inpatient facilities to appoint a **medical safety manager** (iryō anzen kanrisha) who supports the safety committee and, when the facility manager so directs, delivers all or part of the staff training under item (iii).

MHLW's implementation notice of March 31, 2026 (医政地発0331第1号) says the medical safety manager must be a full-time employee with sufficient knowledge of medical safety. A health care license is not required, but where an unlicensed person is appointed the facility must arrange support from licensed staff. In a hospital the role cannot be combined with that of the hospital manager, though it can be combined with roles such as drug safety manager ([MHLW notice of March 31, 2026, implementation points](https://www.mhlw.go.jp/content/10800000/001687485.pdf)). MHLW recommends the manager attend training that follows its program guideline for medical safety manager training.

The same ordinance adds a new Article 1-10-6 from **April 1, 2029**. It requires hospitals, and clinics and midwifery homes with inpatient facilities that perform a set level of surgery or deliveries, to have the staff involved in responding to medical accidents attend training on appropriate response to medical accidents, or attend it themselves.

The implementation notice defines the clinic threshold as a combined 120 or more general anesthesia operations or deliveries a year (April to March); all hospitals are in scope regardless of volume. Qualifying training must be run by the Medical Accident Investigation and Support Center, a regional council or a support organization following MHLW's program guideline, and training on the investigation system taken before April 1, 2026 counts. As at November 2026 this obligation has not yet commenced.

sections.heading: Do special functioning hospitals have extra training duties?

blocks.text: Yes. Article 9-20-2 of the Enforcement Regulation adds duties for special functioning hospitals (tokutei kinō byōin), the advanced care hospitals approved by the Minister. Item (xii) requires staff training beyond the Article 1-11 training, covering the hospital's additional safety systems, matters raised by its audit committee, and the knowledge and skills physicians, pharmacists, nurses and other staff need to collaborate in providing advanced care. Item (xiii) requires the hospital manager and the medical safety, drug safety and device safety responsible persons to receive medical safety training periodically.

Item (ix) also links reporting to training: where staff reporting of inpatient deaths and unexpected events to the medical safety department is inadequate, the safety committee must train and guide staff on appropriate reporting. Item (x) requires mutual peer review with another special functioning hospital at least once a year.

blocks.text: Because two notices drive frequency, a single annual calendar with two fixed sessions that cover both medical safety and infection control content is a common way to show compliance. Article 1-11(1)(vi) separately requires records of medical safety management to be maintained. See [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) for record design.

sections.heading: How is compliance checked and enforced?

blocks.text: Compliance is checked through on-site inspections (tachiiri kensa) by the prefectural governor, or the mayor of a city with a health center or a special ward. Article 25(1) of the Medical Care Act lets them order reports and have officials enter a facility to inspect its staffing, cleanliness, structure, medical records, books and documents. The Minister inspects special functioning hospitals under Article 25(3).

Where a facility's operations breach the law or are seriously inappropriate, Article 24-2 allows the governor to order corrective measures within a deadline and, if the order is ignored, to suspend all or part of the facility's business. Training attendance records are therefore operational evidence, not paperwork for its own sake.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Article 1-11, the 2026 and 2007 MHLW notices and the facility's own safety guideline as linked obligations, then defines learning outcomes and assessment points for each before any training is written. When a notice changes, as the medical safety section did in March 2026, the affected outcomes and records are flagged for review rather than rebuilt from scratch.

faqs.q: Is twice-yearly medical safety training a legal requirement in Japan?
faqs.a: The ordinance requires the training but not its frequency. The "about twice a year" expectation comes from MHLW Health Policy Bureau notices, issued as technical advice to prefectures. Inspectors use those notices, so in practice facilities treat two sessions a year as the baseline and add extra sessions after serious incidents or system changes.

faqs.q: Can outpatient clinics meet the requirement with external training?
faqs.a: Yes. MHLW guidance lets clinics without inpatient beds and midwifery homes without inpatient facilities substitute training attended outside the facility, for both medical safety and infection control. The attendance should still be about twice a year plus as needed, and the clinic should keep its own record of what was attended.

faqs.q: Does the medical safety manager need to be a doctor or nurse?
faqs.a: No. MHLW's March 2026 implementation notice says no health care license is required, but the person must be a full-time employee with sufficient knowledge of medical safety. If an unlicensed person is appointed, the facility must arrange support from licensed staff. In a hospital, the hospital manager cannot hold the role.

faqs.q: Can one session cover both medical safety and infection control?
faqs.a: The 2007 MHLW notice allows infection control measures to be implemented together with the general medical safety measures. A combined session can work if it genuinely covers both topics and the attendance record lists both, so each duty can be shown separately at inspection.
